passages.title: Caught
passages.intro: Read the two texts below, then answer questions 1–8. Some questions ask about both texts.
passages.credit: Both texts were written for this practice test.
paragraphs: The flags were up: red and yellow, planted in the sand like a promise. Between them the water was a flat, friendly blue. Beyond them, to the left, it looked even calmer – a smooth, dark lane where no waves broke at all. That was what Jess noticed first, because it was wrong. Calm water on a surf beach is never just calm.

Then she saw the boy. He was small, maybe seven, sitting on a boogie board in the smooth lane and drifting outwards as gently as a leaf on a pond. He was not paddling. He was not waving. He was simply getting smaller.

Jess's legs wanted to run straight into the water. Her head, which had sat through three summers of Sunday-morning nippers, told them to wait. Coach Ray's voice was suddenly as clear as if he were standing behind her: 'You can't help anyone if you become the second person who needs saving.'

So she did the thing that felt slowest. She raised her arm high and kept it there, waving it from side to side until a figure in a red and yellow cap on the tower stood up. Only then did she grab her own board, paddle out on the far side of the dark lane and come in towards the boy from the side, the way she had practised a hundred times on days when it had seemed pointless.

'Hold on to the board,' she said, and was surprised at how ordinary her voice sounded. 'Don't swim. We're just going to float for a bit.' The boy's eyes were enormous, but he held on. Behind her she heard the roar of the rescue boat.
TEXT B – from an information leaflet

A rip current is a strong channel of water flowing away from the shore. Rips form when waves push water up the beach and that water finds the easiest path back out to sea. Because the water is moving outwards, waves often do not break over a rip, so it can look like the calmest, safest place to swim. This is exactly why rips catch so many people.

Most people caught in a rip are not dragged under: they are carried away from the beach. Danger comes when a swimmer panics and tries to swim straight back against the current, which can be faster than an Olympic swimmer. Exhausted swimmers are the ones who get into trouble.

Surf lifesavers teach a simple plan: stay calm, float, and raise one arm to signal for help. If you see someone else caught in a rip, do not swim out to them unless you have training and something that floats. Alert a lifesaver or call for help first. A would-be rescuer who has to be rescued doubles the problem.

passages.text:
For centuries, sailors told stories of giant waves that rose out of calm seas and {1} ships without warning. Scientists {2} these tales as exaggerations: according to their calculations, such enormous waves should occur only once in thousands of years.

Then, on New Year's Day in 1995, an instrument on an oil platform in the North Sea recorded a single wave 26 metres high. The evidence was {3}. Researchers began to take the sailors' accounts {4}, and within a few years satellite images had {5} that these 'rogue waves' are far more common than anyone had believed.

Rogue waves are thought to form when several smaller waves {6} and combine their energy. Ships are now designed to {7} much greater forces, and forecasters are working on ways to {8} where rogue waves are most likely to appear.

passages.title: “Hope” is the thing with feathers
passages.intro: Read the poem below, then answer questions 17–22. Lines are numbered. (Gale: a very strong wind; abash: shame or silence; Extremity: the hardest, most desperate times.)
passages.credit: Emily Dickinson, written about 1861, first published 1891. Public domain.
stanzas: And sings the tune without the words –
And sweetest – in the Gale – is heard –
And sore must be the storm –
That could abash the little Bird
I’ve heard it in the chillest land –
It asked a crumb – of Me.

passages.title: The Rocks That Walk
passages.intro: Six paragraphs have been removed from the article. Choose the paragraph (A–G) that best fits each gap (questions 23–28). There is one extra paragraph you do not need.
passages.credit: Original article written for this practice test.
paragraphs: In a remote dry lakebed in California's Death Valley, called Racetrack Playa, rocks move by themselves. Some weigh as much as a person, yet each one leaves a long, shallow trail behind it in the cracked mud, as if something had dragged it across the ground. For decades, nobody had ever seen one move.

That was the challenge two cousins, Richard and James Norris, decided to take on in 2011. They placed rocks fitted with GPS trackers on the playa and set up a weather station and cameras. Then they waited – for more than two years.

bank.A: Over the years, people suggested all kinds of explanations. Some blamed hurricane-force winds; others suggested magnetism, slippery algae, or simply pranksters pushing the rocks around at night.
bank.B: The trouble was that none of these ideas could be tested without actually watching a rock move. And the rocks seemed to move so rarely that a scientist could visit for years without seeing a thing.
bank.C: Their patience was rewarded in December 2013. After a rare winter rain, the playa was covered by a shallow pond. On cold nights, a thin sheet of ice formed on its surface, as thin as a windowpane.
bank.D: On sunny mornings the ice began to crack into large floating panels. Even a light breeze was enough to push these panels across the pond, and the panels shoved the rocks along in front of them through the soft mud.
bank.E: The rocks did not race. They crept along at a few metres per minute, so slowly that a person standing nearby might not notice. Some travelled more than 200 metres before the ice melted and the water dried up.
bank.F: The mystery that had puzzled visitors for nearly a century had a surprisingly gentle answer: not powerful winds or magic, but thin ice, a breeze and a lot of patience.
bank.G: Death Valley is one of the hottest places on Earth, with summer temperatures that can reach more than 50 °C.

passages.title: Getting It Wrong
passages.intro: Read the four extracts about mistakes. For questions 29–38, choose which extract (A, B, C or D) each statement matches. You can use each letter more than once.
passages.credit: Original texts written for this practice test.

A.title: The Lucky Burn (a chef's memoir)
A.text: In my first week as head chef, I left a tray of caramel on the stove for far too long while I argued with a delivery driver. By the time I ran back, it had turned the colour of strong tea and smelled like a campfire. I was about to throw it out when an old waiter dipped a spoon in and said, 'Put salt in that and serve it with apples.' Twenty years later, burnt-salt caramel is still the most popular dessert on our menu. I have stopped pretending it was my idea.

B.title: The Mould That Saved Millions (a science magazine)
B.text: In 1928 the scientist Alexander Fleming returned from a holiday to find that mould had grown on one of the dishes of bacteria he had left on his bench. Around the mould, the bacteria had died. A less curious researcher might have scrubbed the dish clean. Fleming studied it instead, and the substance the mould produced, penicillin, became the first widely used antibiotic. Other scientists later did the hard work of making it in large amounts, a reminder that a lucky accident is only the beginning.

C.title: We Lost Again (a junior coach's blog)
C.text: Our under-11s lost 6–0 on Saturday, which is a slight improvement on last week's 9–0. Some parents have suggested the problem is the new kit. It isn't. The problem is that we panic and all chase the ball like seagulls after a chip. So this week we are practising one thing: staying in position. Losing is not the disaster people think it is, as long as you are willing to look honestly at why it happened.

D.title: Review: 'Glorious Failures'
D.text: This book promises to celebrate history's great mistakes, and some chapters, especially the one on failed flying machines, are genuinely fascinating. Too often, though, the author treats every disaster as a joke, and seems to forget that some of these 'glorious failures' cost people their savings, their health or worse. It is possible to learn from mistakes without making fun of the people who made them.

questions.stem: What idea is found in BOTH texts?

options.A: Water that looks calm on a surf beach may actually be dangerous.
options.B: Children should never use boogie boards at the beach.
options.C: Rips are most dangerous on sunny days.
options.D: Surf lifesavers should always be the first people to enter the water.

questions.explanation: Text A: Jess notices the calm, dark lane is 'wrong'. Text B: waves don't break over a rip, so it 'can look like the calmest, safest place to swim'. Both warn that calm-looking water can be a rip.

distractors.B: neither text says this
distractors.C: neither text mentions sunny days
distractors.D: Text B tells ordinary people to alert lifesavers, but neither text says lifesavers must always go first

questions.skill: How one text explains the other
questions.stem: Which part of Text B best explains why Jess waved her arm before going into the water?

options.A: Rips form when waves push water up the beach.
options.B: A would-be rescuer who has to be rescued doubles the problem.
options.C: Most people caught in a rip are not dragged under.
options.D: A rip current can be faster than an Olympic swimmer.

questions.explanation: Jess remembers Coach Ray: you can't help anyone if you become 'the second person who needs saving'. Text B gives the same reason: a rescuer who needs rescuing doubles the problem. So she signalled for help first.

distractors.A: explains how rips form, not why she waved
distractors.C: true, but not why she signalled first
distractors.D: explains why swimming against a rip is hard, not why she waited

questions.stem: Jess tells the boy 'Don't swim. We're just going to float for a bit.' Which advice in Text B does this follow?

options.A: Swim straight back to the shore as fast as possible.
options.B: Only swim between the flags.
options.C: Stay calm and float rather than swimming against the current.
options.D: Call for help before going near the water.

questions.explanation: Text B says to stay calm and float, and that swimming against the current exhausts people. Jess tells the boy to float and not swim.

distractors.A: Text B warns against this
distractors.B: Text B doesn't give this advice, and it doesn't match what Jess says to the boy
distractors.D: Jess did this earlier, but it's not what she says to the boy

questions.stem: The boy drifts outwards 'as gently as a leaf on a pond' (Text A, paragraph 3). What is the effect of this comparison?

options.A: It shows that the boy is enjoying himself.
options.B: It suggests that the water is shallow.
options.C: It shows that the boy is about to fall off his board.
options.D: It makes the danger seem peaceful and quiet, which makes it more frightening.

questions.explanation: A leaf on a pond is calm and harmless. Describing the boy's drift this way shows how quietly the rip is taking him: there is no splashing or shouting, which is what makes it so dangerous.

distractors.A: he isn't waving or paddling, but nothing says he's enjoying it
distractors.B: a pond suggests stillness, not depth
distractors.C: the image is of gentle drifting, not falling

questions.stem: 'Jess's legs wanted to run straight into the water. Her head … told them to wait.' (Text A, paragraph 4). This shows that Jess

options.A: is too frightened to help the boy.
options.B: does not care what happens to the boy.
options.C: cannot decide whether the boy is really in trouble.
options.D: has to fight her instinct to rush in and instead follow her training.

questions.explanation: Her 'legs' stand for her instinct to rush in; her 'head' remembers her training. She chooses the training, even though it feels slow.

distractors.A: she does help, after signalling
distractors.B: her urge to run in shows she cares
distractors.C: she has already realised the water is 'wrong' and the boy is drifting

questions.stem: Why does Jess paddle out 'on the far side of the dark lane' and come towards the boy from the side?

options.A: Because the boy asked her to come from that direction.
options.B: Because the flags told her to swim there.
options.C: So that she won't be caught in the same current that is carrying the boy away.
options.D: So that the lifesaver on the tower could see her better.

questions.explanation: The dark lane is the rip. Paddling around it and approaching from the side keeps Jess out of the strongest current, matching Text B's warning about rescuers needing rescue.

distractors.A: the boy doesn't speak
distractors.B: the flags mark where to swim, not how to reach the boy
distractors.D: she has already signalled the tower

questions.stem: Jess 'was surprised at how ordinary her voice sounded' (paragraph 6). What does this suggest?

options.A: She is calmer on the outside than she feels inside, which helps keep the boy calm.
options.B: She is bored by the rescue.
options.C: She is annoyed with the boy for drifting out.
options.D: She has lost her voice from shouting.

questions.explanation: She expects to sound frightened but sounds normal. Her calm voice is exactly what the boy needs, and it shows her training working.

distractors.B: the situation is tense, not boring
distractors.C: nothing suggests annoyance
distractors.D: she speaks clearly

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of Text B?

options.A: to tell an exciting story about a rescue
options.B: to explain what rips are and how to respond to them safely
options.C: to persuade people to join a surf lifesaving club
options.D: to argue that beaches should be closed when there are rips

questions.explanation: Text B explains how rips form, why they look calm, why people get into trouble, and what to do: it informs and advises.

distractors.A: that is Text A
distractors.C: it mentions lifesavers but doesn't ask people to join
distractors.D: it gives advice, not an argument for closing beaches

questions.stem: Gap 1: choose the best word.

options.A: soaked
options.B: flooded
options.C: drowned
options.D: swamped

questions.explanation: 'Swamped' means overwhelmed with water: a giant wave swamps a ship.

distractors.A: 'soaked' is used for people or clothes getting wet
distractors.B: places flood; a wave doesn't 'flood' a ship
distractors.C: people drown, not ships

questions.stem: Gap 2: choose the best word.

options.A: discarded
options.B: denied
options.C: dismissed
options.D: deleted

questions.explanation: To 'dismiss' a story as an exaggeration means to treat it as not worth believing.

distractors.A: you discard objects you throw away
distractors.B: you deny that something happened, but 'denied these tales as exaggerations' isn't English
distractors.D: you delete files or words

questions.stem: Gap 3: choose the best word.

options.A: unavoidable
options.B: undeniable
options.C: uncertain
options.D: unlikely

questions.explanation: A measured 26-metre wave is proof that can't be argued with: the evidence was undeniable.

distractors.A: unavoidable means impossible to escape
distractors.C: the opposite: the instrument measured it
distractors.D: it actually happened

questions.stem: Gap 4: choose the best word.

options.A: seriously
options.B: strictly
options.C: severely
options.D: sincerely

questions.explanation: 'Take something seriously' means treat it as true and important.

distractors.B: 'take strictly' isn't a phrase
distractors.C: 'take severely' isn't a phrase
distractors.D: you can mean something sincerely, but not 'take' it sincerely

questions.stem: Gap 5: choose the best word.

options.A: convinced
options.B: concluded
options.C: contained
options.D: confirmed

questions.explanation: Satellite images 'confirmed' (proved) that rogue waves are common.

distractors.A: you convince a person, not 'convinced that'
distractors.B: people conclude; images don't
distractors.C: contained means held inside

questions.stem: Gap 6: choose the best word.

options.A: overflow
options.B: overlap
options.C: overtake
options.D: overturn

questions.explanation: Waves that 'overlap' sit on top of each other and add their energy together.

distractors.A: overflow is when a container spills
distractors.C: overtake means pass
distractors.D: overturn means tip over

questions.stem: Gap 7: choose the best word.

options.A: withstand
options.B: withdraw
options.C: withhold
options.D: within

questions.explanation: 'Withstand' means survive or resist a force.

distractors.B: withdraw means pull back
distractors.C: withhold means keep back
distractors.D: 'within' is not a verb

questions.stem: Gap 8: choose the best word.

options.A: prevent
options.B: pretend
options.C: predict
options.D: protect

questions.explanation: Forecasters 'predict' where waves are likely to appear.

distractors.A: you can't prevent a wave
distractors.B: pretend doesn't fit
distractors.D: 'protect where waves appear' doesn't make sense

questions.stem: Throughout the poem, hope is described as

options.A: a storm that blows across the sea.
options.B: a small bird that lives inside a person.
options.C: a song that the poet learned as a child.
options.D: a warm coat that protects people from the cold.

questions.explanation: Hope has 'feathers', 'perches', 'sings' and is called 'the little Bird': the whole poem develops one metaphor of hope as a bird in the soul.

distractors.A: the storm is what hope survives, not hope itself
distractors.C: the bird sings a tune, but hope isn't a remembered song
distractors.D: the bird 'kept so many warm', but hope isn't a coat

questions.stem: What does 'sings the tune without the words' (line 3) suggest about hope?

options.A: Hope is a feeling people have even when they can't explain it in words.
options.B: Hope is very quiet and hard to hear.
options.C: The poet has forgotten the words to a song.
options.D: Hope only comes to people who can sing.

questions.explanation: A tune without words is felt rather than explained. Hope works the same way: it lifts us even when we can't say exactly why.

distractors.B: line 5 says it is 'sweetest' and clearly heard in a gale
distractors.C: took the line literally
distractors.D: nothing about people needing to sing

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the second stanza (lines 5–8)?

options.A: Hope disappears whenever life becomes difficult.
options.B: Birds often die in storms at sea.
options.C: The poet was once caught in a storm and kept warm by a bird.
options.D: Hope is most comforting in hard times, and only a terrible storm could silence it.

questions.explanation: Hope sounds 'sweetest' in the 'Gale' (hard times), and the storm would have to be very 'sore' (severe) to 'abash' (silence) the bird that has comforted so many people.

distractors.A: the opposite: it is sweetest in the gale
distractors.B: the bird is a metaphor; the stanza isn't about real birds dying
distractors.C: the stanza is figurative, not a real memory

questions.stem: Why does the poet use the words 'chillest land' and 'strangest Sea' (lines 9–10)?

options.A: to describe real places the poet visited on holiday
options.B: to show that birds can fly over land and sea
options.C: to show that hope stays with people even in the coldest, loneliest and most unfamiliar situations
options.D: to suggest that hope only exists in faraway places

questions.explanation: These are images of the hardest, most unfamiliar times in life. The speaker has 'heard' hope even there.

distractors.A: the places are figurative, not travel memories
distractors.B: the point is about hope, not real birds' flight
distractors.D: hope is in 'the soul', not only far away

questions.stem: What do the last two lines ('Yet – never – in Extremity, / It asked a crumb – of Me.') suggest about hope?

options.A: The speaker forgot to feed the bird.
options.B: Hope gives comfort freely and asks nothing in return, even in the worst times.
options.C: Hope eventually becomes hungry and leaves.
options.D: The speaker feels guilty for not looking after hope.

questions.explanation: A real bird would need food. This bird never asked even 'a crumb', even in 'Extremity'. Hope helps us without needing anything back.

distractors.A: took 'crumb' literally
distractors.C: it never asked for anything, so it doesn't leave
distractors.D: the tone is grateful, not guilty

questions.stem: The poet uses many dashes ( – ) instead of full stops and commas. What is the most likely effect?

options.A: They show that the poem is unfinished.
options.B: They show where the bird stops singing.
options.C: They create pauses that make the reader slow down and think about each idea.
options.D: They make the poem rhyme.

questions.explanation: The dashes break lines into small pieces and create pauses, so each image (the feathers, the gale, the crumb) is given weight. Dickinson used them in almost all her poems.

distractors.A: the poem is complete
distractors.B: the bird 'never stops – at all'
distractors.D: rhyme comes from word sounds, not punctuation

options.B: The trouble was that none of these ideas could be tested without actually watching a rock move. And the rocks seemed to move so rarely that a scientist could visit for years without seeing a thing.
options.C: Their patience was rewarded in December 2013. After a rare winter rain, the playa was covered by a shallow pond. On cold nights, a thin sheet of ice formed on its surface, as thin as a windowpane.
options.D: On sunny mornings the ice began to crack into large floating panels. Even a light breeze was enough to push these panels across the pond, and the panels shoved the rocks along in front of them through the soft mud.
options.E: The rocks did not race. They crept along at a few metres per minute, so slowly that a person standing nearby might not notice. Some travelled more than 200 metres before the ice melted and the water dried up.
options.F: The mystery that had puzzled visitors for nearly a century had a surprisingly gentle answer: not powerful winds or magic, but thin ice, a breeze and a lot of patience.
options.G: Death Valley is one of the hottest places on Earth, with summer temperatures that can reach more than 50 °C.

questions.explanation: F is a concluding paragraph that sums up the answer to the mystery, so it belongs at the end.
